title: Knee pain in growing athletes: Osgood-Schlatter disease
excerpt: What's causing the pain below your kneecap, and how to manage it so you can keep playing.
seo: Osgood-Schlatter Disease: Knee Pain in Kids | Solevo
meta: Osgood-Schlatter disease causes knee pain in active kids during growth spurts. What helps, how to manage training load and when to see a physio.
body:
Has your child been complaining of pain just below their kneecap during or after sport? It could be Osgood-Schlatter disease, a common cause of knee pain in active children and adolescents, particularly during growth spurts.

It occurs when the tendon below the kneecap becomes irritated where it attaches to the growing shin bone. Repetitive running, jumping and kicking can place extra stress on this area, causing pain and sometimes a noticeable bump below the knee.

Stopping activity isn't always necessary, but pushing through ongoing pain without appropriate management can prolong symptoms and affect sporting performance.

What you should do about it

  • Activity modification: Scale back high-impact activities when needed and work out an appropriate training load to avoid aggravating symptoms.
  • Knee support: Taping, sleeves or patellar straps may help improve comfort during activity.
  • Quad and hamstring strength: Controlled single-leg exercises help build strength and capacity for the demands of sport.
  • Stretching and mobility: Focus on the quads, hamstrings, calves and hip flexors to address muscle tightness.
  • Balance work: Single-leg exercises improve balance, coordination and control for sport.

When should you seek help?

If your child is experiencing ongoing knee pain, particularly during or after sport, it's worth getting it assessed. Pain that limits activity, causes swelling or makes everyday movements uncomfortable shouldn't be ignored.

title: Heel pain that holds you back: meet Sever's disease
excerpt: Why growing heels get sore, and how to stay active without making it worse.
seo: Sever's Disease: Heel Pain in Active Kids | Solevo
meta: Sever's disease is a common cause of heel pain in growing kids who play sport. How to manage load, footwear and strength, and when to see a physio.
alt: Legs on a step beside an exercise ball during a calf exercise
body:
Is your child complaining of heel pain when running, jumping or playing sport? It could be Sever's disease, one of the most common causes of heel pain in growing children and adolescents.

Sever's disease is the irritation of the growth plate at the back of the heel bone. During growth spurts, the combination of growing bones, tight muscles and repetitive impact from sport can place extra stress on this area, causing pain.

While symptoms may ease with rest, they can return when activity resumes. Pushing through ongoing pain can prolong recovery and affect the way your child runs, jumps and moves.

What you should do about it

  • Rest and load management: Work with your physio to find the right balance between activity and recovery. Some children may need a temporary break from high-impact sport.
  • Footwear and cushioning: Supportive shoes and heel cups can help reduce impact and improve comfort.
  • Calf and lower leg strength: Strengthening the muscles involved in running and jumping helps the legs cope with sporting demands.
  • Stretching and mobility: Gentle calf and ankle stretches can help address tightness, provided they don't cause pain.
  • Balance work: Single-leg exercises improve stability, control and movement.

When should you seek help?

If your child is experiencing ongoing or recurring heel pain, particularly during or after sport, it's worth getting it checked. Pain that causes limping, limits activity or makes everyday walking uncomfortable shouldn't be ignored.

title: Shin splints or bone stress? Know the difference
excerpt: Both cause shin pain, but knowing what's happening can make a big difference to your recovery.
seo: Shin Splints or Bone Stress Injury? | Solevo Physio
meta: Shin splints and bone stress injuries both cause shin pain but need different care. How to tell them apart, manage your load and return to running.
alt: Runner holding a sore shin on a running track
body:
Experiencing shin pain during or after running? It could be shin splints or a bone stress injury. While the two conditions can feel similar, they affect different structures and require different management.

Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) involve irritation and sensitivity along the inner border of the shin bone, usually due to repetitive loading. Pain is often spread over a broader area and commonly develops with running or increased training loads.

Bone stress injuries occur when repetitive loading exceeds the bone's ability to repair itself. These injuries range in severity, from early stress reactions to stress fractures. Pain is often more localised, can worsen as activity continues and may eventually occur during everyday walking or even at rest.

How you can manage shin pain

  • Manage your load: Reduce or modify aggravating activities, particularly running and jumping, while symptoms settle.
  • Don't push through pain: Continuing to train through a suspected bone stress injury can worsen the injury and delay recovery.
  • Build strength: Gradually strengthen your calves, hips and lower limbs to improve your capacity to handle sporting demands.
  • Return gradually: Increase running volume and intensity progressively once symptoms and injury severity allow.

When should you seek help?

If shin pain is persistent, worsening, localised to one spot or starting to affect everyday walking, it's important to get it assessed. A physiotherapist can help identify the likely cause, guide appropriate load management and determine whether further investigation or medical review is needed.

Don't ignore shin pain and hope it disappears. Our physio team can help identify what's going on and guide your return to running safely. Book now!

title: Achilles pain? Don't let it slow you down
excerpt: Why your Achilles tendon gets sore and how to rebuild its strength so you can get back to running, walking and doing what you love.
seo: Achilles Pain: How to Rebuild Strength | Solevo Physio
meta: Achilles pain or morning stiffness? Why the tendon gets sore, how load management and calf strengthening help, and when to see a physio in Brookvale.
alt: Calf raises on a step to strengthen the Achilles tendon
body:
Experiencing pain or stiffness at the back of your ankle, particularly first thing in the morning, walking upstairs or starting a run? It could be Achilles tendinopathy, a common condition affecting the tendon that connects your calf muscles to your heel bone.

Your Achilles tendon plays an important role in walking, running and jumping. When the demands placed on it exceed its ability to cope, it can become painful and less tolerant to activity. This often happens following changes in training load or increased repetitive activity.

Symptoms commonly include morning stiffness, tenderness through the tendon and pain during or after exercise. The good news is that with the right load management and progressive strengthening, you can rebuild tendon capacity and get back to doing what you love.

How you can manage your Achilles

  • Load management: Temporarily adjust running, jumping and other aggravating activities rather than stopping all activity. Finding the right balance is key.
  • Calf strengthening: Progressive calf raises, including straight and bent-knee variations, help rebuild the strength and capacity of the Achilles tendon.
  • Gradual progression: Increase exercise resistance and activity levels as your strength and symptoms improve. Rushing back into sport can cause symptoms to flare up.
  • Return to sport: Gradually reintroduce running, jumping and higher-impact activities once your tendon has built up enough strength to tolerate them.

When should you seek help?

If Achilles pain is lingering, returning regularly or starting to affect your walking, running or exercise, it's worth getting it assessed. A physiotherapist can help you safely return to activity.

title: Why heel pain may be costing you your distance
excerpt: How plantar fasciopathy can affect your walking, balance and golf swing.
seo: Heel Pain and Your Golf Swing | Solevo Physio
meta: Heel pain from plantar fasciopathy can shorten your stride and weaken your golf swing. What helps, from stretching to strength, and when to get it checked.
body:
That first step out of bed in the morning, or after a few holes of golf, shouldn't feel like stepping on a knife. If it does, plantar fasciopathy could be the reason your stride feels shorter and your swing less powerful.

Often called plantar fasciitis, it's a condition affecting the thick band of tissue that supports the arch of your foot. Despite its common name, it isn't usually an inflammatory condition but involves changes to the tissue in response to repeated loading.

Increased activity, reduced calf strength, limited ankle mobility and changes in training load can all contribute to the problem. The result is often sharp, stabbing pain through the heel or arch, particularly with those first steps in the morning or after walking the course.

When heel pain sets in, your walking pattern, balance and ability to push off can all be affected. This can influence weight transfer and movement through your golf swing, potentially impacting power and consistency.

How to manage your heel pain

  • Calf and plantar fascia stretching: Gentle calf stretches and plantar fascia-specific stretches can help manage stiffness and discomfort, particularly first thing in the morning.
  • Foot and calf strength: Exercises such as calf raises and short-foot exercises help build strength and improve the foot's ability to tolerate load.
  • Load management: Temporarily adjusting walking distances, training loads and time on the course can help settle symptoms while maintaining activity where possible.
  • Manual therapy: Hands-on treatment targeting the calf and foot may help improve comfort and mobility as part of a broader rehabilitation program.

When should you seek help?

If heel pain is lingering, returning regularly or starting to affect your walking, exercise or golf, it's worth having it assessed by a physiotherapist. We share our Brookvale clinic with The Foot Company podiatrists, so foot problems can be assessed together.

title: Over 60? Don't let strength slip away
excerpt: Why maintaining muscle and strength as you age is key to staying active, independent and doing the things you love.
seo: Over 60? Don't Let Strength Slip Away | Solevo Physio
meta: Losing strength after 60 is common but not inevitable. How strength training helps you stay active and independent, and where to start safely.
alt: Older woman lifting light dumbbells at home
body:
Have you noticed everyday activities becoming a little harder? Getting out of a chair, carrying the shopping or climbing stairs might not feel as easy as they once did. As we age, we naturally begin to lose muscle mass and strength, a process known as sarcopenia.

This can start from around midlife and become more noticeable as we get older, particularly if we're less physically active. Reduced muscle strength can affect everything from walking and balance to everyday tasks and maintaining independence.

The good news is that muscle strength can be improved at any age. Regular strength training helps maintain muscle mass, improve physical function and give your body the capacity to keep up with the demands of everyday life.

How you can improve your strength

  • Strength training: Incorporate resistance exercises targeting major muscle groups, including your legs, hips, back and arms. Even simple exercises can make a difference.
  • Start with the basics: Exercises such as sit-to-stands, step-ups and resistance band work are great ways to build strength and improve everyday function.
  • Progress gradually: As your strength improves, gradually increase resistance or exercise difficulty to keep challenging your muscles.
  • Stay consistent: Aim to include strength training at least twice a week. Regular exercise is more beneficial than occasional bursts of activity.

When should you seek help?

If you're noticing a loss of strength, struggling with everyday activities or unsure where to start with resistance training, a physiotherapist can help develop a program suited to your ability and goals.

It's never too late to get stronger. Our physio team can help you build strength, maintain independence and keep doing the things you enjoy. Book now!

title: Steady on your feet: why balance matters as you age
excerpt: How improving your strength, balance and confidence can help reduce your risk of falls and keep you doing the things you love.
seo: Why Balance Matters as You Age | Solevo Physio Brookvale
meta: Feeling less steady on your feet? Falls are not an inevitable part of ageing. Exercises that improve balance and strength, and when to get assessed.
alt: Two women doing single-leg balance exercises in a studio
body:
Feeling a little less steady on your feet? Finding it harder to get up from a chair, walk on uneven ground or catch yourself when you lose your balance? These can be signs that your balance and strength need some attention.

While falls become more common as we get older, they aren't an inevitable part of ageing. Changes in muscle strength, coordination, mobility and balance can all increase the risk of falling.

The good news is that losing your balance isn't simply an inevitable part of ageing. Strength, coordination and stability can all be improved with the right exercises and guidance. Maintaining these abilities is important not only for reducing falls risk, but also for staying independent and confident in everyday life.

How you can reduce your falls risk

  • Balance training: Exercises such as single-leg standing and tandem walking help improve stability and control.
  • Build leg strength: Strengthening your quads, glutes and calves supports everyday movements like standing, walking and climbing stairs.
  • Functional exercises: Practising sit-to-stands, stepping and changing direction helps prepare your body for everyday activities.
  • Keep moving: Regular physical activity helps maintain strength, mobility and coordination. Consistency is key!

When should you seek help?

If you've had a fall, feel unsteady when walking or are becoming less confident with everyday activities, it's worth having your balance assessed.

Don't wait until a fall happens to start working on your balance. Our physio team can help you build strength, improve stability and maintain your independence. Book now!
